summary: Defines two new DNS resource record types for NSAP addresses and their reverse lookup, and reserves their type mnemonics and numbers. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 1637.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS is an address book for the Internet. This adds new entry types so it can also hold addresses from a different network system.

questions: how does dns store nsap addresses
subtitle: DNS records to store and look up addresses from non-IP networks.

tldr.problem: The DNS was built for IP addresses, but some hosts need to use other address types, such as OSI NSAP addresses, and DNS needs to store and look them up too.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new DNS resource record types: NSAP (type 22) to map DNS names to NSAP addresses, and NSAP-PTR (type 23) to do reverse lookup from NSAP addresses back to DNS names, analogous to the existing PTR records for IP addresses.
tldr.outcome: This experimental extension was designed for next-generation networks, but wider adoption of IPv6 followed a different path. It was replaced by RFC 1637.

today: RFC 1348 is Experimental. It was superseded by RFC 1637, which provides an updated specification for DNS NSAP records.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs NSAP Records
sections.content: RFC 1348 defines two new DNS resource record types to extend the Domain Name System beyond IP addresses. Some systems want to run Internet applications (TCP and UDP) on top of CLNP (the OSI Connectionless Network Protocol), which uses NSAP (Network Service Access Point) addresses instead of 32-bit IP addresses. DNS needs a way to store these longer addresses and allow reverse lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers use a different numbering system for addresses, and DNS needs to be able to write them down and look them up.

sections.title: The NSAP and NSAP-PTR Record Types
sections.content:
The NSAP resource record (type code 22) stores the actual NSAP address. It has the form <owner> <ttl> <class> NSAP <length> <NSAP-address>. The length field specifies the number of octets in the NSAP address, which varies by the national and international authority that assigned it. The address itself is encoded as a character string.

The NSAP-PTR record (type code 23) provides the reverse function, similar to the IPv4 PTR records in in-addr.arpa. It maps from an NSAP suffix back to a DNS name, allowing reverse lookups in a domain tree analogous to nsap-in-addr.arpa.
sections.plainLanguage: NSAP stores an address from another network system, and NSAP-PTR does the reverse, finding the name when you start with the address.

sections.title: Purpose and Status
sections.content: This RFC was designed to support a next-generation Internet protocol proposal that would use longer addresses. The two record types provide the infrastructure for DNS to work with CLNP and other OSI-based systems. The RFC updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, the core DNS specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: These new DNS records were made for an experimental new version of the Internet that never became the main one, but they laid groundwork for DNS to handle different address types.
